stories.headline: House Ethics Committee Opens Investigation Into Rep. Jimmy Gomez Over Sexual Misconduct Allegations
stories.summary:
The House Ethics Committee announced Monday that it is investigating Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) over allegations of sexual misconduct, including alleged inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer. The panel said it is "reviewing allegations" that Gomez "may have engaged in sexual misconduct in violation of the Code of Official Conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct."

Gomez issued a statement acknowledging he made "personal mistakes outside my marriage" but maintained his actions were consensual and did not violate the law or House Ethics rules. The California Democrat did not provide additional details about the nature of the allegations.

The investigation makes Gomez the latest House member to face Ethics Committee scrutiny over alleged sexual misconduct, amid ongoing calls from members of both parties to tighten Congress's rules around workplace conduct. The probe was reported across multiple outlets representing a range of editorial perspectives, signaling broad newsworthiness.

The Ethics Committee investigation does not constitute a finding of wrongdoing, and the panel's review could result in a range of outcomes from dismissal to formal disciplinary recommendations. No timeline for the investigation was announced.

stories.headline: Norway's King Harald V Hospitalized, Crown Prince Haakon Named Regent
stories.summary:
Norway's King Harald V, 89, was admitted to hospital Monday and placed on two weeks of sick leave, the country's royal household announced. The palace said the monarch, one of Europe's longest-reigning sovereigns, was hospitalized due to "fluid retention in the body that requires treatment," following recent treatment with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a rare blood condition that reduces red blood cell count and causes fatigue and shortness of breath.

Crown Prince Haakon, 53, will serve as regent during his father's hospitalization. King Harald has ruled Norway since January 1991 and has publicly ruled out abdication despite a series of health setbacks in recent years, including a pacemaker fitting in 2024 and hospitalization in the Canary Islands for infection and dehydration in February.

The latest hospitalization adds to a difficult period for the Norwegian royal family. Queen Sonja was admitted to hospital in May for heart-related examinations. The family has also faced public scrutiny over Crown Princess Mette-Marit's past correspondence with Jeffrey Epstein and the rape conviction of her son Marius Borg Høiby in June.

Norway's monarchy remains a constitutional institution with largely ceremonial powers, but the king's repeated health crises and the regent transition carry significance for national continuity and public attention to royal succession.

stories.headline: Sydney Swans AFL Players Under Police Investigation for Alleged Sexual Assault at Melbourne Hotel
stories.summary:
Several Sydney Swans players from Australia's premier football competition are under investigation by Victoria Police following an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in East Melbourne in the early hours of Sunday morning. The Swans confirmed that an incident involving an unspecified number of players had occurred after the team's win at Melbourne Cricket Ground.

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich said the club was "still piecing together exactly what's transpired" and described leadership as "extremely shocked and disappointed." He declined to specify the number of players involved, whether arrests had been made, or the precise nature of the allegations, citing the active police investigation.

Victoria Police confirmed detectives are investigating a report of sexual assault at a hotel on Wellington Parade but said "the exact circumstances are yet to be established." The AFL said it had been made aware of the matter and was monitoring the police investigation.

The incident comes at a sensitive moment for the club, which sits second on the 2026 ladder with 17 wins from 22 games and is heading into the finals. The case echoes previous high-profile misconduct scandals in Australian rules football and is drawing significant public attention in Australia.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Seizes Cargo Ships in Strait of Hormuz as U.S. Declares Blockade
stories.summary:
President Trump declared Monday that the United States is blockading the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran continues to escalate. Iran's top negotiator responded by asserting that Tehran "will decide the right of passage" through the waterway, and Iranian forces seized two cargo ships in the strait, including a Panama-flagged vessel whose engine room was struck by a U.S. military helicopter in the Gulf of Oman.

The confrontation has sent energy markets into sharp swings since the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have both indicated talks have progressed toward allowing some shipments to resume, but Iran has denied Trump's assertion that negotiations are formally under way, leaving the diplomatic situation in flux.

The blockade declaration marks a significant escalation in the ongoing conflict and carries major implications for global oil supply chains and shipping. All 14 crew members aboard one seized Indian-flagged vessel were safely rescued, India's foreign ministry confirmed. The standoff has already pushed unleaded petrol prices in the UK to 160 pence per litre, with broader inflationary consequences rippling through allied economies.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue the blockade is a necessary tool to cut off Iranian revenues and force a negotiated resolution to Tehran's nuclear program and regional aggression. Critics warn that interdicting one of the world's most vital shipping lanes risks a broader military confrontation and could trigger a global recession through sustained oil supply disruption.

stories.headline: CDC Reports Kindergarten Vaccine Exemptions Rose to 4.2% in 2025-2026 School Year
stories.summary:
Vaccination rates among American kindergartners declined across all tracked vaccines during the 2025-2026 school year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported Monday. Exemptions from one or more vaccines increased in 41 states and the District of Columbia, rising to 4.2 percent from 3.6 percent the prior year — a trend that puts measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) coverage below the threshold needed to prevent widespread outbreaks.

The decline coincides with continued Trump administration efforts to revise federal vaccine policy, including changes championed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Public health experts warn that falling coverage, combined with measles case counts already at levels not seen in years, increases the risk of outbreaks in school-age populations across the country.

The data represent a national public health concern because herd immunity for measles typically requires vaccination rates above 95 percent. Falling below that threshold in a growing number of states leaves communities — particularly those with young children who cannot yet be vaccinated — vulnerable to resurgent disease.

Supporters of expanded exemption policies argue that parental choice and informed consent should govern vaccine decisions, and that some exemptions reflect legitimate medical or religious concerns. Public health officials and pediatric medical groups counter that the aggregate decline in coverage poses a collective risk that outweighs individual preferences, and are calling on federal and state authorities to reverse the trend.

stories.headline: Justice Dept. Inspector General Opens Review of DEA Tactic That Let Fentanyl Reach Streets
stories.summary:
The Justice Department's internal watchdog announced Monday it will review a controversial DEA investigative tactic in which federal agents monitored — but deliberately did not seize — major fentanyl shipments in order to build larger prosecutorial cases against drug trafficking networks. The review was disclosed by Inspector General Don Berthiaume, one of his first official actions since being sworn in Friday.

The announcement follows an Associated Press investigation published less than two months ago that found DEA agents repeatedly stood down on significant fentanyl deliveries in New Mexico between 2023 and 2025. Internal DEA records reviewed by AP showed agents watched and declined to interdict a single delivery of 74,000 fentanyl pills at an Albuquerque mobile home park. DEA whistleblower Agent David Howell told AP that authorities "poisoned our community to make cases."

The tactic — sometimes called allowing drugs to "walk" — is used across federal law enforcement to avoid compromising wiretap investigations and to pursue higher-level targets. Current and former agents say the strategy amounts to a gamble with public safety that may have violated Justice Department rules designed to protect communities from what the White House last year designated a "weapon of mass destruction." The IG review will cover the past two years and could determine whether similar stand-downs occurred in other cities.

DEA Administrator Terry Cole had previously requested a narrower inspector general inquiry following AP's reporting, saying the request should not be interpreted as a lack of confidence in DEA personnel. The broader review announced Monday goes further than Cole's request. Howell said he expects the review to confirm that federal authorities "endangered the public through willful inaction."

stories.headline: White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt Resigns; Succession Questions Arise
stories.summary:
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt announced she is resigning from her position to focus on her family, creating an immediate vacancy in one of the most publicly visible roles in the Trump administration. The departure was confirmed Monday, with no successor publicly named as of the announcement.

Leavitt, who became the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary when she was appointed at the start of Trump's second term, was a prominent and combative public face for the administration throughout its first year and a half. Her exit comes at a consequential moment, with midterm elections approaching and the administration managing multiple active international crises including the U.S.-Iran conflict and ongoing Strait of Hormuz tensions.

Former White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer noted the intense pressure the role carries, describing the job as one of the most scrutinized positions in government. The selection of a replacement is expected to be closely watched as a signal of how the administration intends to manage its public communications heading into the midterm campaign season.

No immediate reaction from senior Democratic leadership was available. The White House had not announced a timeline for naming a successor as of Monday afternoon.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Pauses Border Wall Construction Inside Big Bend National Park
stories.summary:
The Trump administration announced Monday it has temporarily halted border wall construction inside Big Bend National Park in Texas, with U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott saying he ordered the pause to conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation of the project. Scott announced the decision via social media, stating he would visit the site before any construction resumes.

The project has drawn unusually broad bipartisan criticism, with both Republican and Democratic lawmakers pushing back against building a border barrier inside one of the country's most remote and ecologically sensitive national parks. Critics argue the construction has been rushed and is causing environmental damage to a pristine wilderness area along the Rio Grande.

Supporters of the administration's overall border security agenda argue that operational control of the southern border must extend to all terrain, including national parks, where illegal crossings have historically been difficult to monitor. The pause does not signal a cancellation of the project, and CBP's evaluation will determine next steps.

The decision reflects broader tensions within the administration's border enforcement push over how to balance security priorities with environmental and legal constraints. A federal judge separately ruled against a Native American tribe's trespassing claims related to a nearby Arizona border construction project, citing a 1907 land proclamation.

stories.headline: Tupac Shakur Murder Trial Opens With Opening Statements Nearly 30 Years After Killing
stories.summary:
Opening statements began Monday in Las Vegas in the murder trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the first person charged in the 1996 drive-by shooting death of rapper Tupac Shakur. Davis was indicted in 2023, nearly three decades after Shakur was shot at a stoplight following a Mike Tyson boxing match on September 7, 1996, and died six days later.

Davis, who had previously given media interviews in which he discussed his knowledge of the killing, faces a murder charge as the alleged organizer of the ambush. Prosecutors are expected to argue he coordinated the attack from the back seat of the vehicle from which shots were fired.

The case has drawn intense public interest as one of hip-hop's most enduring unsolved mysteries nears a legal reckoning. Defense attorneys are expected to challenge the reliability of evidence gathered over nearly three decades and question whether Davis's own prior public statements are admissible.

stories.headline: French Prime Minister Heckled During Visit to Wildfire-Devastated Region as Blazes Continue Across Europe
stories.summary:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was heckled Monday during a visit to Le Porge in southwestern France, where 183 homes burned in recent wildfires. About 200 residents gathered at the town hall, with a local advocacy group organizer alleging they were blocked from meeting with the prime minister by lines of riot police, while Lecornu's office said it had "nothing to hide" about how fire operations were conducted.

Lecornu announced €12 million in aid for the Gironde and Landes regions, pledging to issue building permits for equivalent reconstruction of destroyed homes within a month. Residents expressed anger over how the fires were managed, with one local questioning why professional firefighters left to defend another area while only volunteer firefighters remained.

Wildfires continued to burn across Europe on Monday, with Belgian authorities reporting that the largest wildfire in the country's recent history, burning in the Hautes Fagnes nature reserve, had continued to spread overnight before stabilizing somewhat due to more favorable winds. Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden deployed air support to assist Belgian firefighting teams.

In Greece, authorities reported 41 forest fires ignited in the past 24 hours, with ongoing blazes requiring active response, as the country remained on high fire alert.

stories.headline: Russia Sentences Last Registered Anti-War Politician to 11 Years, Bans His Party from September Elections
stories.summary:
A Russian court in Pskov sentenced Lev Shlosberg, the deputy head of the liberal Yabloko party and the country's most prominent remaining anti-war politician, to 11 years and one month in a penal colony on Monday. He was convicted of "discrediting" Russia's armed forces and "spreading false information" about them, charges stemming from social media posts. The verdict was handed down minutes before Russia's Supreme Court separately rejected Yabloko's appeal against a ban on participating in September's parliamentary elections.

Shlosberg, 63, condemned the ruling as politically motivated, telling the court its only purpose was to "punish a person for his political, public and civil position." He was repeatedly interrupted by the presiding judge during his closing statement, in which he again called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and political dialogue. Yabloko said it would appeal the sentence.

Yabloko was the only registered Russian party to oppose the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched in 2022. Its exclusion from September's elections—justified by authorities on grounds including alleged support for the "international LGBT movement" and copyright infringement—leaves all 10 remaining parties on the ballot as supporters of the war. Independent election watchdogs have been largely stripped of their ability to monitor the process.

The sentencing marks a significant escalation in the Kremlin's suppression of domestic dissent ahead of the September 18-20 parliamentary vote. Shlosberg's imprisonment removes the last prominent legal opposition voice inside Russia, reinforcing the wartime censorship apparatus that has effectively criminalized public criticism of the military campaign in Ukraine.

stories.headline: Lake Powell Hits Record Low, Threatening Water and Power for 40 Million in Seven States
stories.summary:
Lake Powell, the United States' second-largest reservoir, dropped to a record low elevation of 3,519.91 feet above sea level on Saturday, edging below the previous record set in April 2023. The milestone comes roughly a week after the Colorado River's other major reservoir, Lake Mead, also hit a historic low. Together, the two reservoirs now hold less combined water than at any point since the Glen Canyon Dam was under construction in May 1957.

The Colorado River Basin is the primary water source for more than 40 million people across seven states—California, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and Colorado—and supports significant hydroelectric power generation. Lake Powell is now approximately 30 feet above the elevation at which its turbines would stop producing electricity. Federal officials warned in April that a "major intervention" would be needed to avoid that threshold by year's end.

Persistent overuse of the river, a record-dry winter, and rising temperatures have driven the depletion. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation proposed a 10-year management plan in July that includes potentially significant water cuts for Arizona, California and Nevada, but the federal government and the seven basin states have yet to reach agreement on a long-term framework.

The crisis is already affecting Lake Powell's tourism economy, forcing marina relocations, closure of boat ramps, and adaptation across the recreational industry. Scientists and retired water officials who published a recent analysis of the combined reservoir data say levels may continue to fall, making a negotiated solution increasingly urgent.

stories.headline: Record Rainfall Triggers Fatal Landslide in South Korea as Storms Batter East Asia
stories.summary:
A landslide struck an apartment building in the South Korean city of Geoje on Monday morning following record-breaking rainfall, killing one person and injuring two others. Rescuers pulled three residents from the buried ground floor of the building. Geoje recorded 124.5mm of rainfall in a single hour—the highest one-hour total since meteorological records for the city began in 1972—with more than 400mm falling overnight between Sunday and Monday.

The disaster is part of a broader pattern of extreme weather striking East and Southeast Asia this month. Back-to-back storms have caused widespread flooding and landslides across South Korea, China, Japan and the Philippines. Japan's Chiba prefecture near Tokyo recorded "unprecedented" rainfall last week that killed 10 people, stranded thousands at Narita Airport and cut power to more than 20,000 households. Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in eastern China on Monday, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to Shanghai and surrounding areas.

Forecasters attribute the unusually intense typhoon season to a strong El Niño pattern that began in June, which raises global temperatures and increases the destructive power of typhoons. Multiple storms sweeping through the region in rapid succession have strained emergency response capacity and damaged infrastructure across several countries simultaneously.

South Korean city authorities have closed tourist attractions in Geoje and suspended bus operations and waste collection due to flooded or damaged roads. Residents were urged on Sunday to avoid driving and stay away from riverbanks as further rain continues to threaten the region.

stories.headline: UK Prime Minister Burnham Exchanged Messages With Impersonator Posing as Trump's Chief of Staff Susie Wiles
stories.summary:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham communicated with an unknown individual impersonating Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff and one of President Trump's closest advisers, according to people familiar with the matter. The incident raises immediate national security concerns about the new prime minister's communications protocols and vetting procedures for high-level contacts.

Four outlets including Bloomberg, CBS News, the New York Post, and The Guardian are covering the story. Accounts differ slightly in tone: the Guardian described the suspicious activity as having been identified quickly with no messages of significance exchanged, while the New York Post characterized it as Burnham stumbling into a national security gaffe shortly after taking office.

The episode is politically embarrassing for Burnham's government at a sensitive moment in UK-US relations, particularly as Britain navigates diplomacy with the Trump administration. It is not yet clear who was behind the impersonation, what the perpetrator's motive was, or how the suspicious contact was ultimately flagged and terminated.

stories.headline: Fed Minutes, Walmart and Home Depot Earnings headline a Major Week for Wall Street Amid Persistent Inflation
stories.summary:
Wall Street faces a consequential week with earnings reports from four of the nation's largest retailers — Home Depot on Tuesday, Target and Lowe's on Wednesday, and Walmart on Thursday — along with the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve's most recent policy meeting on Wednesday. Investors and economists are watching the results closely for signals about how businesses and consumers are coping with inflation that remains solidly above 3 percent.

The ongoing U.S. war with Iran has driven a surge in oil prices, pushing up gasoline costs and raising prices on a wide range of goods. Results from home improvement retailers could shed light on housing market conditions, while Walmart and Target figures will offer a clearer picture of household budgeting and discretionary spending under sustained price pressure.

The Fed held interest rates steady at its July meeting, though three officials dissented in favor of higher rates — a rift Fed Chair Kevin Warsh publicly called a 'good family fight.' Wall Street currently anticipates at least one rate hike before year's end, and the release of meeting minutes may clarify how close policymakers are to pulling that trigger.

stories.headline: What Happens to the Personal Information You Share With AI Chatbots
stories.summary:
A new Axios investigation examines the largely unregulated landscape governing how artificial intelligence companies handle sensitive personal information shared by users during chatbot conversations. The report highlights a scenario with few legal guardrails: a chatbot designed to maximize engagement or influence purchasing decisions could potentially draw on fears, insecurities, and private disclosures a user has shared to tailor its responses.

The investigation focuses on the promises made by major AI companies — including OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic — about consumer data use, noting that those promises carry outsized weight precisely because formal regulatory requirements remain sparse. Questions about data retention, secondary use of personal disclosures, and whether AI systems can leverage intimate user information for commercial ends are at the center of the inquiry.

The story comes as concern grows among educators, policymakers, and consumer advocates about AI's rapid integration into daily life. Separately, the New York Times is also reporting on the issue, indicating growing mainstream attention to the gap between AI companies' self-described data policies and what users actually understand about the fate of what they share.

stories.headline: Update: Indonesia Earthquake Death Toll Rises to 68 as Aid Shortages and Starvation Fears Mount in Flores
stories.summary:
A 7.7-magnitude earthquake that struck the Indonesian island of Flores on Saturday has now killed at least 68 people and displaced approximately 5,000, making it the country's deadliest quake since 2022. Landslides have severed access roads to the hardest-hit villages, cutting off survivors from rescue teams, food, and medical supplies. Thousands remain sleeping outdoors in makeshift shelters, fearing further collapses as aftershocks continue to rattle the region.

The acute shortage of medical personnel has emerged as a critical crisis. Dr. Melinda, the sole physician at the decimated Dampek Health Centre, posted an urgent appeal describing herself as unable to cope with hundreds of casualties arriving around the clock without rest. Ruteng Regional General Hospital, roughly four hours from the worst-hit areas, has also reported that promised medical assistance had not yet arrived.

More than 1,000 houses were damaged, along with dozens of health facilities, schools, and government offices, according to Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency. Search-and-rescue teams are still working to reach cut-off communities, and officials warn the full casualty count may not yet be known. The death toll has risen from the 53 previously reported, representing a material new development in an ongoing disaster.

stories.headline: Hurricane Lala Sweeps Away About 100 Homes in Hawaii, Knocks Out Power to 219,000
stories.summary:
Hurricane Lala skirted the Big Island of Hawaii on Saturday and Sunday, delivering catastrophic flash flooding and mudslides without making direct landfall. Roughly 100 or more homes were uprooted from their foundations by torrents of water, and more than 219,000 households lost electricity. Three hospitals also lost power, though backup generators kept them operational. Governor Josh Green said there were, 'amazingly,' no confirmed fatalities linked directly to the home destruction, though one person died in a car accident.

The storm dumped as much as 32 inches of rain in some areas, with its eyewall passing within 30 miles of South Point overnight. Wind speeds peaked at 91 mph before Lala weakened to a tropical storm tracking westward, south of the islands. Tropical storm warnings remained in effect for all eight of Hawaii's major islands on Sunday, and the governor deployed approximately 180 National Guard members to assist with emergency response.

Both of Big Island's main airports — Hilo International and Ellison Onizuka Kona — were temporarily closed, with some 190 flights postponed. Maui residents faced water supply disruptions. Hawaii has not seen a hurricane make landfall since Category 4 Hurricane Iniki struck Kauai in 1992, causing six deaths and $3 billion in damage. Officials warned the danger was not yet over as the storm continued to track near the island chain.

stories.headline: Zambian Security Forces Raid Opposition Leader's Home on Election Day After Shootout
stories.summary:
Zambian security forces raided the residence of the country's main opposition leader on the day of the presidential election, arresting 11 people following a shootout. Authorities described the operation as part of an investigation into an alleged plot involving foreign nationals. The incident drew immediate scrutiny from international observers monitoring the election.

President Hakainde Hichilema appeared on course for an outright re-election victory, according to early reports, but election observers noted violence and what they characterized as a tilted campaign environment. The raid on the opposition leader's home on election day raised concerns about political interference and the integrity of the democratic process in one of southern Africa's historically more stable democracies.

Zambia has been regarded as a regional model for peaceful transfers of power since its independence era, making the armed raid and shootout at an opposition leader's compound during voting a significant and alarming development. International observers and regional bodies had been monitoring the election, and their assessments of the pre-election environment and the day's events are expected to shape the international response to the outcome.

stories.headline: Actress Hayden Panettiere, Star of 'Nashville' and 'Heroes,' Dies at 36
stories.summary:
Hayden Panettiere, the actress best known for her roles as cheerleader Claire Bennet in the NBC series 'Heroes' and country music star Juliette Barnes in 'Nashville,' has died at age 36. Her representative confirmed the death to ABC News. Panettiere had worked in entertainment since infancy, appearing in commercials at 11 months old, and built a long career as a child and adult actress.

In May 2026, Panettiere published a memoir chronicling a turbulent decade that included battles with depression and substance abuse, stints in rehabilitation, and losing custody of her daughter Kaya, whom she shares with former fiancé and professional boxer Wladimir Klitschko. She had spoken publicly in recent years about her struggles and her efforts toward recovery. Tributes from the entertainment industry poured in following the announcement of her death.

Panettiere's death was reported by seven major outlets, making it one of the most widely covered stories of the day. She was 36 years old.
